title: Suno Studio’s October update meets the work creators already do
question: How might Suno’s recent Studio changes affect an independent musician turning generated material into a release?
argument: Suno announced tools for aligning, stretching and fading clips. Those changes address editing tasks, but the available creator accounts show why hands-on direction and cleanup still matter. Neither creator account tests the October update.
synthesis: Suno’s release note says Studio now offers improved downbeat detection, clip stretching and shaped fades. Separately, a musician describes generating material to cut into samples, while a video creator describes removing noise from stems in Studio. Together, these sources suggest that clip editing could matter to creators who treat Suno output as material to arrange and refine. They cannot show whether the October changes improve those creators’ results, save time or make a track ready to release.
limitations: The feature description comes from Suno’s product marketing. The musician’s account and the video document individual practices, not representative outcomes or tests of the October changes. Independent tests of the new tools and perspectives from creators who decided against releasing their results are missing.

claims.statement: Suno announced improved first-downbeat detection for newly created Studio clips and said it reduces the need to align non-rhythmic clips manually.

locator.quote: We’ve made improvements to the detection of beat 1 in new clip creations. This means the timing of clips and takes on the Studio timeline is greatly improved, and there is more accuracy around the first downbeat in a clip. Now, the experience of working with non rhythmic clips, such as a cappella vocals, is smoother and the need to manually align is reduced.

claims.statement: Suno also announced shift-click-drag clip stretching and adjustable fade curves in Studio.

locator.quote: We’ve added a new feature where shift-click-dragging automatically timestretches a clip.
Now, you can shape the curve by dragging the node on the fade icon to create exponential- and logarithmic-shaped fades.

claims.statement: In a MusicRadar interview, producer Todd Edwards described generating material with Suno Studio, then cutting it up for use as samples. His account describes his own workflow; it does not establish that the resulting material is legally cleared.

locator.quote: But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples, and never worry about another lawsuit again—because it’s mine, all of it.

claims.statement: A YouTube creator described cutting noisy portions from stems in Studio and adding EQ and compression to a vocal channel. This documents one creator’s editing process, not a test of the October features.

The October tools could help musicians who cut generated material into samples or clean and arrange stems, because they give users more control over clip timing and transitions. The sources do not establish that either documented creator used the new tools or obtained a better result from them.

locator.quote: Improvements to Studio: Tighter timing, clip stretching and fade curves.
But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples

title: What Suno Quality Tests Actually Measure
question: Do current tests show that Suno gives independent musicians better sound and more control?
argument: The supplied tests answer narrower questions than an overall quality verdict. WaveDisco measured loudness and peaks across three songs. Ytyng measured spectral and dynamic properties across exports made under different conditions. Two YouTube creators tested whether particular inputs and directions produced results they liked. Their methods can reveal useful behavior, but they do not establish a general v6 quality score.
synthesis: WaveDisco’s same-prompt comparison found no consistent LUFS or True Peak improvement, while ytyng’s exported tracks showed less high-frequency energy in its v6 set. These findings can coexist: they measure different properties, and ytyng’s older and newer tracks used different prompts and codecs. The YouTube demonstrations add a separate question: whether a result follows a creator’s melody or performance directions. Together, the sources suggest that release readiness needs listening and inspection of the specific output, not a single model ranking. None establishes an average result across creators, genres, or exports.
limitations: WaveDisco’s format comparison covers two songs. Ytyng’s older and newer sets differ in songs, prompts, and codec. The YouTube demonstrations use individual songs and creator judgments rather than blinded listening tests. The lyric-direction creator also acknowledges that ordinary generation variation could explain the perceived improvement. The supplied evidence lacks a broad, independently run test with matched prompts, settings, exports, and listener ratings; a creator testing their own intended release remains the missing perspective.

claims.statement: WaveDisco’s author regenerated three songs across four model versions with the same lyrics and prompt, then measured LUFS and True Peak. The author found no consistent direction in those measures that would justify an overall claim that v6 sounded better.

locator.quote: Three songs, four model versions each, same lyrics and prompt every time. I measured LUFS and True Peak on every output with the same audio analysis pipeline, and compared WAV and MP3 formats where I had both.
On LUFS and True Peak, I didn't find one — the numbers move, but there's no consistent direction I can point to.

claims.statement: In the two songs with format comparisons, WaveDisco reported a WAV–MP3 loudness gap for v5.5 and no LUFS gap for the three v6 variants. That is a finding about those exports, not an aesthetic verdict or a guaranteed model behavior.

locator.quote: On v6-mini, v6-wild, and v6: the LUFS difference is zero across all three.
To be clear: this is two songs where I had format comparisons. It's an illustration, not a study. Your tracks may behave differently.

claims.statement: Ytyng measured 24 v6 exports against 12 older exports and reported lower high-frequency energy in the v6 set. The author says the songs and prompts were not controlled and the sets used different codecs, so the measurement cannot isolate a model-version effect.

locator.quote: v6 was down 2 to 3.4dB at 2 to 12kHz, and the spectral centroid was 36% lower.
The biggest one is that the songs and genres are not controlled. The v6 side is 2 songs and the pre-v6 side is 6 songs, each made from a different prompt.
the v6 side is m4a (Opus 132kbps) and the pre-v6 side is mp3 (about 180kbps VBR), and I compare them as they are.

claims.statement: The lyric-direction YouTube creator kept the style the same while adding performance, vocal, and instrument directions, and judged one version’s vocals clearer. The creator later conceded that generation variation might account for the difference, so the demonstration supports a workflow to try rather than a proven control effect.

Andrea Olsen of Produce Like a Boss uploaded one of her own voice memos and judged that Suno kept its melody while producing an output she could still identify as AI. Her test assesses fidelity to her particular input and her listening judgment; she also promotes music-business training, a relevant commercial incentive.

The mismatch between the tests is methodological: WaveDisco’s loudness and peak measurements do not answer ytyng’s spectral question, and neither answers whether Suno preserved Olsen’s melody or followed the lyric-direction creator’s performance instructions. The evidence therefore supports testing the property a songwriter cares about on their own exports, while leaving overall musical quality unresolved.

locator.quote: I measured LUFS and True Peak on every output with the same audio analysis pipeline
For the measurement I decoded with ffmpeg and ran an FFT.

title: Before a Suno-assisted release, trace what you contributed and where the recording will go
question: What should an independent creator verify before uploading a demo or releasing a Suno-assisted track, and what evidence should they watch next?
argument: Build a record of the human-written and generated parts, check the applicable Suno terms before uploading or distributing, and confirm how the destination platform treats the finished track. Treat licensing promises, lawsuits and an opened investigation according to their stated status.
synthesis: A creator can make these checks concrete: Josh of JG Beats Lab proposes retaining the demo, lyrics, settings, stems, vocal takes and master; Andrea Olsen demonstrates uploading her own voice memo while urging attention to the terms; Music Business Worldwide reports Suno’s account that user creations contributed to v6 training. Together, these sources support checking both the material supplied to Suno and the record of human contribution. They do not establish how a particular upload was used in training or what rights attach to a particular output. The Italian authority’s investigation and Deezer’s planned search filter add reasons to watch contract terms and distribution rules, but neither establishes a legal finding or a discoverability outcome for a specific Suno-assisted song.
limitations: The supplied material does not include the applicable primary Suno terms, a court decision on the new complaint, a completed Italian investigation, or a platform classification of a specific release. The podcast host teaches a workflow, and Olsen sells music education; their practical steps are attributable advice, not legal determinations. Independent musicians’ concerns are represented, but the terms and outcomes of individual artist payments remain undisclosed.

claims.statement: Josh, founder of JG Beats Lab, recommends keeping a song folder with the original demo, lyrics, settings, selected stems, raw vocal takes and final master, then marking which parts were written or generated. This is a practitioner’s documentation method, not proof of ownership.

In her video demonstration, producer and music educator Andrea Olsen uploads a voice memo she says is her own and urges creators to examine terms before uploading songs. Her video also promotes an IP service and a paid course, so its legal characterizations require checking against primary terms.

Music Business Worldwide reports that Suno described v6 training as including licensed partner content and community interactions, including creations and preference signals. That is Suno’s account of its training inputs, not a finding about the use of any one creator’s file.

locator.quote: v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team.

claims.statement: The Los Angeles Times reports that participating label deals promise artist choice and payment, while payout terms and the number of artists opting in have not been disclosed. A creator should therefore seek terms for the specific arrangement rather than assume a partnership settles individual consent or compensation.

locator.quote: But so far, none of them have disclosed what artists will be paid, how many artists have opted in, or how much input individual musicians have over whether their work is used.
It’s also not always clear whether opting out keeps an artist’s recordings out of AI training, or only out of fan-facing features.

claims.statement: The Italian Competition Authority opened an investigation into Suno’s terms, raising possible concerns about contractual changes, accounts and content, and the scope of the copyright license. An investigation states issues under examination; it is not an adverse finding.

locator.quote: The Italian Competition Authority has launched an investigation into Suno Inc., a US company that provides generative AI services specialising in music creation. The proceedings focus on Suno’s Terms of Service.

The scope of the license imposed on consumers as a condition for using the platform services seems to be insufficiently defined, as it is framed in generic and all-encompassing terms, and imposes the waiver of moral rights contrary to Articles 20 et seq. of Law 633/1941.

claims.statement: Music Business Worldwide reports that Sony and Universal’s new complaint accuses Suno of copying recordings, while Suno calls the claims flawed. These are opposing positions in litigation, not a decision that a creator’s release infringes.

locator.quote: The new complaint filed on Friday, obtained by MBW, accuses Suno of copying 60,202 of the labels’ sound recordings without a license.
“These claims remain fundamentally flawed on both the facts and the law,” Suno said in a statement issued to media, adding that “Suno exists so that more people can make new music.”

claims.statement: Dazed reports Zemi’s account that he sings and produces material before using Suno to change his voice. His description shows why a creator may need to document the specific human and generated parts of a track, though it does not independently verify his process.

locator.quote: “Yes, the voice is AI, but all the rest is produced by me – the beats, the top lines, the production,” Zemi explains. “I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself. The entire process behind it is human.”

claims.statement: Deezer says it plans to roll out a search toggle for fully AI-generated music before the end of 2026. A creator considering Deezer distribution should watch the eventual rule and classification of their track; the report does not show that the toggle is live or that it covers every AI-assisted song.

locator.quote: Deezer says it is introducing an on/off toggle that will let users exclude fully AI-generated music from their search results.
The French streaming service said on Tuesday (October 13) that the feature will roll out globally before the end of 2026.

claims.statement: Taken together, the practitioner documentation method, Suno’s reported training account and the Italian authority’s scrutiny of license scope support a pre-upload check: identify what the demo contains, retain evidence of human contributions, and inspect the applicable terms before supplying it. These sources cannot determine the legal effect of a particular upload.

locator.quote: v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team.

The scope of the license imposed on consumers as a condition for using the platform services seems to be insufficiently defined, as it is framed in generic and all-encompassing terms, and imposes the waiver of moral rights contrary to Articles 20 et seq. of Law 633/1941.
